design_detail: Systematic review of population-based longitudinal studies (cohorts, or case-control studies nested in cohorts) of cannabis use and later psychotic or affective outcomes, with DerSimonian and Laird random-effects meta-analysis of adjusted odds ratios where studies were judged homogeneous enough, and narrative synthesis otherwise. Ten databases searched from inception to 5 September 2006 without language limits. 35 reports included: 11 on psychosis from 7 cohorts and 24 on affective outcomes (depression, depressive symptoms, suicidal ideation or attempts, anxiety) from 15 cohorts. Funded by the UK Department of Health.
can_establish: The average adjusted association, in general-population cohorts published up to 2006, between ever use or the most frequent use of cannabis and later psychotic outcomes (mostly self-reported or interview-rated psychotic symptoms; three cohorts with a psychotic-disorder outcome) and depression, and how much adjustment for measured confounders reduced each cohort's crude association.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes psychosis or depression (all included studies are observational, and the authors state that confounding or bias cannot be ruled out), the size of any causal effect, effects of potency or of age at first use (no robust data), or absolute risks (none are pooled; the lifetime risk of less than 3% in the conclusion is given without a source).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Medline, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, ISI Web of Knowledge, ISI Proceedings, ZETOC, BIOSIS, LILACS and MEDCARIB from inception to 5 September 2006, plus reference lists of included studies and other reviews, and letters to experts and study investigators for published and unpublished studies (pp. 319-320). Psychosis cohorts: five adult population cohorts (ECA, USA; EDSP, Germany; NEMESIS, Netherlands; NPMS, UK; 1969 Swedish conscripts) and two New Zealand birth cohorts (Dunedin; Christchurch, CHDS). Affective cohorts: the two birth cohorts, six adult population cohorts (Berkeley, ECA and New York state, USA; NPMS, UK; Northern Rivers, NoRMHS, Australia; Colombia) and seven school-based cohorts (Victoria, Australia; AddHealth, Baltimore, Chicago, LA schools, LAT and NY schools, USA) (pp. 320-321).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: population-based longitudinal studies or case-control studies nested within them. Excluded: cohorts of people with mental illness or substance-use problems, prison populations, and randomized trials of cannabis for medical use (different pharmacokinetics from recreational cannabis, short follow-up). Every psychosis outcome required delusions, hallucinations or thought disorder (schizophrenia and related disorders, affective or non-affective psychoses, psychotic symptoms); affective outcomes covered mood and bipolar disorders, depression, suicidal ideation or attempts, anxiety, neurosis and mania. Search restricted to human studies, not by language or design (pp. 319-320).
sample.demographics: Not given in the article: per-study sample sizes, ages, sex and follow-up are in webtables 1 and 2 (online supplement, not read). The main text gives country and cohort type only.
sample.attrition: Within the included cohorts: loss to follow-up 4% to 32% in the psychosis cohorts (no attrition data for the Swedish conscripts), and 4% to 70% (median 20%) in the affective cohorts, not reported for two. The authors judge from attrition modelling in CHDS, NEMESIS and NoRMHS that attrition had little effect on the findings (pp. 322, 324, 326).
sample.selection_effects: General-population cohorts by design, which avoids the clinical selection of case-control and cross-sectional samples. The psychosis evidence rests on seven cohorts, two of them (Dunedin, CHDS) with additional analyses supplied by the investigators and one Swedish analysis unpublished (Zammit S); the affective NPMS data come from a personal communication. Excluding treatment and psychiatric samples means the review says nothing about people already in services. Per-study data needed to reconstruct the pools are only in the webtables.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported cannabis use measured before the outcome in each cohort; no biological verification. Psychosis analyses: ever use in all cohorts except NPMS, where the measure was use in the past year (Figure 1 legend); most frequent use was daily use in CHDS, ECA and EDSP, weekly use in NEMESIS, dependence in NPMS and use more than 50 times by conscription in the Swedish cohort (Figure 2). Affective analyses used ever use, current use, use less than weekly or at least monthly, at least weekly or heavy use, frequency trends, and cannabis misuse disorder (Figures 3 to 6 legends).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable as dose. The pooled most-frequent-use estimates combine categories ranging from more than 50 lifetime occasions to daily use and dependence, so they describe the top category of each cohort, not one exposure level. Route not reported. The authors note large variation in the cannabinoid content people actually take in and error in self-reported frequency (p. 325).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled through each study's own adjustment. The discussion states that all psychosis studies reporting an association adjusted for other drug use (two not for alcohol), but Figure 2 marks three of the six most-frequent-use estimates (EDSP, NEMESIS, NPMS) as not adjusted for other drug use (see reporting issues). Roughly half the affective studies made no adjustment for alcohol or other drug use. The authors note that under-reporting of stimulant use, which is commoner in people who use cannabis, could inflate associations (p. 326).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Intoxication at outcome assessment was addressed only partly: the interview instruments used in ECA, NEMESIS, Dunedin and EDSP instruct the interviewer to exclude symptoms arising solely from drug use; the SCL-90 (CHDS) and the psychosis screening questionnaire (NPMS) cannot separate intoxication; no affective study explicitly excluded intoxication or withdrawal effects (pp. 322, 324-325).

comparison.controls: People in the same cohorts who had never used cannabis (ever-use estimates) or did not use it (most-frequent-use estimates).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Adjusted estimates from each study's own models were pooled. About 60 confounders were adjusted for across the psychosis studies (other substance use, personality traits, sociodemographic markers, intellectual ability, other mental-health problems) and about 50 across the affective studies (family and peer relationships, adverse life events, criminality, mental-health problems, sociodemographic markers, other substance use); the set used by each study is in the webtables (not read).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychotic symptoms at baseline were excluded (ECA, NEMESIS, NPMS, Swedish conscripts) or adjusted for (EDSP, Dunedin, CHDS), but three psychosis studies (EDSP, NEMESIS, Dunedin) made no adjustment for other mental disorders at baseline, two (NEMESIS, Dunedin) none for alcohol, and the authors judge the baseline tools unlikely to capture all symptoms (p. 325). Family history of psychosis, genetic liability, childhood adversity and sub-threshold prodromal symptoms are not discussed as adjustment variables. For affective outcomes, only four studies excluded people with affective symptoms at baseline and seven neither excluded nor adjusted (p. 324).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported per study; comparison groups were defined by cannabis use only.

outcomes.instruments: Psychosis: SCL-90 (CHDS), Diagnostic Interview Schedule (Dunedin, ECA), Munich CIDI (EDSP), CIDI (NEMESIS), psychosis screening questionnaire (NPMS), ICD clinical diagnosis of schizophrenia at hospital admission (Swedish conscripts) (Table 1). Affective: CES-D, DIS, DISC, CIDI, CIS-R, SCL-90, Hopkins symptom checklist, an NIMH interview, and DSM or ICD-10 diagnoses (Table 2; Figures 3 to 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was assessed descriptively: sampling, response rates, missing data, attrition, and how each study limited reverse causation, intoxication effects and confounding (Tables 1 and 2). No scored tool.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis outcomes were pooled on the stated assumption that they lie on a continuum from self-reported symptoms to a clinical diagnosis of schizophrenia. Six of the seven psychosis cohorts had a symptom outcome without any requirement for impaired functioning; three had a psychotic-disorder outcome with impaired functioning (Dunedin schizophreniform disorder, NEMESIS needs-based diagnosis, Swedish conscripts hospital admission for schizophrenia). Depression outcomes were diagnoses or above-threshold scale scores.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six pooled estimates: four main (any psychotic outcome by ever use and by most frequent use; psychotic disorder by ever use; depression by most frequent use) and two sensitivity analyses omitting NEMESIS. Depressive symptoms, suicidality and anxiety were synthesized narratively.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Eligibility was judged and data extracted independently and in duplicate, with disagreements resolved by consensus; screening of titles and abstracts is not described as duplicate (p. 320).

analysis.effect_sizes: DerSimonian and Laird random-effects pooled adjusted odds ratios (Stata metan), with I-squared and a heterogeneity p value; no tau-squared or prediction intervals. Any psychotic outcome, ever use versus never: OR 1.41 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.65), 7 cohorts, I2 19.2%, heterogeneity p=0.28. Most frequent use versus none: 2.09 (1.54 to 2.84), 6 cohorts, I2 44.1%, p=0.11; without NEMESIS 1.92 (1.50 to 2.47), I2 25.0%, p=0.26. Psychotic disorder, ever use: 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13), 3 cohorts, I2 66.9%, p=0.049; without NEMESIS 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30), I2 48.3%, p=0.16. Depression, most frequent use: 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94), 8 estimates from 7 cohorts, I2 29.6%, p=0.192. Egger test: psychosis p=0.48 (7 studies), depression p=0.13 (10 studies). Adjustment reduced the crude psychosis associations by about 45% on average (range 10% to 80%), measured as the share of the crude excess odds removed. Population attributable fraction, assuming causality and 40% ever use: about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19) of psychotic outcomes in young UK adults.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; the per-study adjustment sets are in the webtables. Because adjusted estimates from different models were pooled, no single adjustment set lies behind a pooled odds ratio.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. Full search details, eligibility record forms, the list of excluded studies and a MOOSE compliance summary are said to be on the authors' departmental website (not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The review did not pool depression by ever use because exposure measures were too heterogeneous (p. 323), yet it pooled depression by most frequent use across at-least-weekly use, at-least-monthly use, heavy use, dependence and misuse disorder, including one unadjusted estimate (NoRMHS). The sensitivity analyses drop NEMESIS because it contributed most to heterogeneity, a data-driven choice. Per-study results behind the narrative syntheses are only in webtable 2.
analysis.power: The authors calculate that more than 230 events were needed for 80% power to detect a depression odds ratio of 1.5 and judge that about half the depression studies were underpowered (p. 323). The publication-bias tests rest on 7 and 10 studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In seven general-population cohorts, ever use of cannabis was associated with 1.41 times the adjusted odds of a later psychotic outcome, mostly self-reported or interview-rated symptoms; the top use category of each cohort (from more than 50 lifetime occasions to daily use or dependence) with 2.09 times the odds; and the three cohorts with a psychotic-disorder outcome gave 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13) with I2 67%, or 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30) without NEMESIS. Adjustment removed on average about 45% of the crude excess odds (10% to 80% by cohort). Four of the seven adjusted ever-use estimates have intervals that exclude 1 (editors' count from Figure 1). Evidence for depression was weaker (most-frequent-use pool 1.49, 1.15 to 1.94) and less protected against reverse causation and confounding; suicidality and anxiety were not pooled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary says the evidence is consistent with the view that cannabis increases the risk of psychotic outcomes independently of confounding and transient intoxication, that results restricted to psychotic disorders were similar, and that there is sufficient evidence to warn young people (p. 319); the conclusion repeats the warning and puts individual lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorder, even with regular use, at "likely to be low (less than 3%)" without a source (p. 327). Gaps: (1) the discussion itself says residual confounding can never be eliminated and that confounding or bias cannot be ruled out (pp. 325, 327), so independence from confounding holds only for the measured confounders; (2) intoxication was addressed in some cohorts only (Table 1); (3) the disorder estimate is nearly twice the any-outcome estimate, rests on three cohorts with substantial heterogeneity and has a lower limit near 1 without NEMESIS, which the word similar understates; (4) the dose-response wording rests on top-use categories that differ between cohorts and include three estimates not adjusted for other drug use. The authors are explicit that their attributable fraction assumes causality (p. 326) and present the warning as a policy judgment under uncertainty (p. 327).

timeline.event: Andreasson et al., Swedish conscript cohort (the review's ref. 28); with the 2002 follow-up by Zammit et al. (ref. 29) and a Zammit PhD thesis (ref. 30) it supplies the review's schizophrenia estimates (ever use 1.50, 1.11 to 2.02; more than 50 times 3.10, 1.72 to 5.58).
Dunedin (Arseneault et al., ref. 31) and NEMESIS (van Os et al., ref. 26) cohorts: the two other psychotic-disorder outcomes in the pooled disorder estimate.
Degenhardt, Hall and Lynskey (ref. 60): schizophrenia incidence has not tracked trends in cannabis use, used as an argument against a causal effect; the review cites it and the reply below.

Earlier syntheses compared in Table 3: Arseneault et al. 2004 (narrative review with meta-analysis), Macleod et al. 2004 (systematic review of psychosocial outcomes, no meta-analysis), Semple et al. 2005 (systematic review), Henquet et al. 2005 (narrative review); the meta-analyses among them included cross-sectional data, unadjusted results or combined ever use with dependence, and all reported larger effects.

Caspi et al. (ref. 32): COMT Val158Met moderation of the cannabis-psychosis association in Dunedin, and Henquet et al. 2006 (ref. 56), an experimental test; the review judges the evidence for this effect modification very weak (both seen only in subgroups).

Hickman et al. (ref. 61): model projections in which time lags and unreliable incidence data mean changes in schizophrenia incidence may not yet be visible; cited by the review against the trends argument.
This review, published with an editorial (p. 292) and a comment (p. 293) in the same Lancet issue (not read).

Gage, Hickman and Zammit (narrative review; Zammit is an author of both) restate this review's three pooled estimates and re-pool ever use with two later cohorts (Zurich, ALSPAC): 1.46 (1.24 to 1.72), I2 19%, methods not given.
Ksir and Hart, critical overview arguing for shared vulnerability; it does not cite this review or the cohorts pooled in it.
Gillespie and Kendler, viewpoint triangulating genetically informed designs: the association is judged partly causal and partly confounded or reverse-causal.

replication.where_it_stands: The first systematic review restricted to longitudinal population studies, and the source of the most quoted pooled figures (1.41 for ever use; 2.09 for the most frequent use). Gage et al. (2016), with Zammit as a shared author, re-pooled with two later cohorts and obtained 1.46 (1.24 to 1.72). The estimates are observational: Gillespie and Kendler (2021) read genetically informed designs as showing an appreciable non-causal share of the association, and Ksir and Hart (2016) argue that the whole association reflects shared vulnerability; neither re-analyses these cohorts. Claims must not count this review and the cohorts pooled in it, or Gage et al.'s re-pooling, as independent support.

funding.funder: Department of Health, UK; Zammit funded through a Clinician Scientist Award from the National Assembly for Wales (Acknowledgments, p. 327). The paper states that the sponsor had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing, and that the corresponding author had full access to the data and final responsibility for submission (Role of the funding source, p. 320).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (p. 327): Jones and Barnes were invited experts on the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs cannabis review in 2005. Zammit, Jones, TJ (initials that match no author), Lewis and Lingford-Hughes have received honoraria for lectures and talks or consultancy fees from pharmaceutical companies, for work unrelated to cannabis. Lingford-Hughes has received an honorarium from Sanofi-Aventis for attending a meeting about cannabinoid antagonists, consultancy fees from Bristol Myers Squibb and unrestricted research monies from Merck. Barnes has received consultancy fees from Servier, Johnson & Johnson and Bristol-Myers Squibb regarding antipsychotic medication. Moore and Burke have no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Universities of Bristol, Cardiff and Cambridge, and Imperial College London. Zammit and Lewis are authors of included reports (the 2002 Swedish conscript follow-up, ref. 29; the NPMS psychosis report, ref. 27), Zammit's PhD thesis (ref. 30) and an unpublished Zammit analysis are used, and the affective NPMS data are a personal communication from a Bristol colleague. Selection and extraction were in duplicate, but no procedure for appraising the authors' own studies is described. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant meta-analysis of general-population cohorts with repeated, biologically checked measures of cannabis use and potency taken before any psychotic symptoms, clinically diagnosed psychotic disorder as the outcome, a common adjustment set (family history, childhood adversity, other drug use, prodromal symptoms) and a sibling or other genetically informed comparison that estimates the part of the association that is familial.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: General-population longitudinal studies; cannabis use (ever, frequency); comparison with no use; psychotic and affective outcomes defined (pp. 319-320).

No protocol or statement that methods were fixed in advance; eligibility forms and a MOOSE summary are said to be on a departmental website. The data-driven sensitivity analyses (omitting NEMESIS) are not justified against a plan.

Restriction to population-based longitudinal studies is explained: medical-cannabis trials differ in pharmacokinetics and follow-up, and earlier reviews were weakened by cross-sectional data (p. 319).

Ten databases including conference-proceedings indexes (ISI Proceedings, ZETOC), no language or design limit, reference lists, letters to experts and investigators for unpublished studies, two PhD theses included; search to September 2006 for a July 2007 publication. Full strategy on a departmental website (not read); the search format is given in the text (p. 320).

Eligibility was judged independently and in duplicate with consensus (p. 320). Title and abstract screening is not described as duplicate; if the item is read as requiring duplicate screening at every stage, it becomes no (non-critical; overall unchanged).
Data extracted independently and in duplicate (pp. 319-320).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 143 full texts excluded, with near misses, are said to be detailed on the senior author's departmental website (p. 320), which was not read; whether each exclusion is justified cannot be judged from the article.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The article gives cohort type, country, exposure and outcome definitions (Figures 1 to 6 legends) and each study's handling of reverse causation, intoxication and confounding (Tables 1 and 2); sample sizes, ages, sex and follow-up are only in webtables 1 and 2 (not read), which may meet the item in full.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Confounding, reverse causation, intoxication, attrition and response were assessed per study (Tables 1 and 2), but measurement of the exposure was not appraised study by study and selection of the reported result was not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of adjusted estimates with stated grounds for pooling (judged homogeneity; a stated continuum of psychosis measures), and no trials mixed in. A close call: the depression pool includes one unadjusted estimate (NoRMHS) without a stated reason, three of the six most-frequent-use psychosis estimates are not adjusted for other drug use, top-use categories differ between cohorts, and no tau-squared or prediction interval is given.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis by study quality (for example excluding cohorts that could not separate intoxication or did not exclude baseline psychosis); the only sensitivity analyses omit NEMESIS for heterogeneity.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion weighs reverse causation, intoxication, residual confounding, attrition and misclassification and states that confounding or bias cannot be ruled out (pp. 325-327).
Heterogeneity is reported for every pool and discussed (the SCL-90 outcome in CHDS; NEMESIS), with sensitivity analyses (pp. 321, 325).
Funnel plots and Egger tests: psychosis p=0.48 (7 studies), depression p=0.13 (10 studies); the authors note the psychosis test rests on only seven studies (pp. 321-322, 325).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, role of the funder and authors' interests are stated (pp. 320, 327); the statement does not flag that review authors wrote included reports.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 (list of excluded studies with reasons) can be judged only from the authors' departmental website, which was not read. With item 2 judged no (no protocol stated), the review has one critical flaw, which gives low confidence; if the excluded-studies list proves missing or unjustified, a second critical flaw would make it critically low. Items 9 (partial yes) and 10 and 12 (no) are further weaknesses. Strengths are real: a broad search without language limits that sought unpublished data, duplicate selection and extraction, restriction to longitudinal population studies, per-study appraisal of reverse causation, intoxication and confounding, random-effects pooling of adjusted estimates and publication-bias tests. The rating concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as summaries; the review remains a sound map of the cohort evidence to 2006, and its pooled odds ratios remain observational associations, as the authors say.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 10 databases from inception to 5 September 2006, no language limit, plus reference lists and contact with experts; 4804 references, of which 175 (3.6%) were read in full and 143 excluded. Included: 11 psychosis reports from 7 cohorts (ECA, EDSP, NEMESIS, NPMS, Swedish conscripts, Dunedin, CHDS) and 24 affective reports from 15 cohorts.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Methods; Methods › Study selection and data collection, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The summary's 35 studies count reports per outcome group (11 + 24); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Any psychotic outcome, ever use versus never use: pooled adjusted OR 1.41 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.65), heterogeneity p=0.28, I2 19.2%, 7 cohorts. Adjusted ORs by cohort (Figure 1): CHDS 1.28 (1.04 to 1.57), Dunedin schizophreniform disorder 2.91 (1.20 to 7.04), ECA 1.30 (0.98 to 1.73), EDSP 1.67 (1.13 to 2.46), NEMESIS 2.11 (0.78 to 5.71), NPMS 0.72 (0.30 to 1.74), Swedish conscripts schizophrenia 1.50 (1.11 to 2.02). Egger test p=0.48. Unadjusted results of all studies showed increased risk, reduced but persisting after adjustment in six.
key_findings.note: Comparison: people who had never used cannabis. Adjustment: each cohort's own confounder set (listed in webtable 1, not read). Exposure was past-year use in NPMS. Persisting in six refers to point estimates above 1; four of the seven adjusted intervals exclude 1 (editors' count). Psychosis outcomes range from self-reported symptoms to hospital diagnosis of schizophrenia.

key_findings.finding: Most frequent use versus no use: pooled adjusted OR 2.09 (1.54 to 2.84), heterogeneity p=0.11, I2 44.1%, 6 cohorts: CHDS daily 1.56 (1.20 to 2.03), ECA daily 2.00 (1.27 to 3.16), EDSP daily 2.23 (1.30 to 3.83), NEMESIS weekly 6.81 (1.79 to 25.91), NPMS dependence 1.47 (0.55 to 3.93), Swedish conscripts more than 50 times 3.10 (1.72 to 5.58). Without NEMESIS: 1.92 (1.50 to 2.47), p=0.26, I2 25.0%. All six studies that examined frequency reported results consistent with a dose-response effect.
key_findings.note: Comparison: people who did not use cannabis. Adjustment: each cohort's own model, but Figure 2 marks the EDSP, NEMESIS and NPMS estimates as not adjusted for other drug use. The top category differs between cohorts (more than 50 lifetime occasions to daily use or dependence).

key_findings.finding: Psychotic disorder (psychotic symptoms with impaired functioning) in three cohorts (Swedish conscripts, hospital admission for schizophrenia; Dunedin, schizophreniform disorder from additional unstratified data supplied by the investigators; NEMESIS, needs-based diagnosis), ever use: pooled adjusted OR 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13), heterogeneity p=0.049, I2 66.9%. Without NEMESIS: 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30), p=0.16, I2 48.3%.
key_findings.note: Comparison: never use; adjustment as in each cohort's own model. The NEMESIS disorder estimate itself is not given in the main text (webtable 1, not read).

key_findings.finding: Age at first use: in Dunedin the effect on psychotic symptoms was stronger for first use before 16, with much weaker evidence for schizophreniform disorder (very wide intervals); in the Swedish conscripts, accounting for cumulative use, risk of schizophrenia did not differ by first use before or after 16. The authors conclude no robust evidence shows that earlier use is more harmful; the Dunedin pattern could reflect greater cumulative exposure.

Putative interactions: in Dunedin, crude OR 10.9 (2.2 to 54.1) for schizophreniform disorder in valine homozygotes at COMT Val158Met versus 1.1 (0.21 to 5.4) in methionine homozygotes, seen only in people who first used before 18. In EDSP the association was stronger in psychosis-prone groups, but these already had psychotic features at baseline. The authors call the evidence for COMT effect modification very weak.

Reverse causation and intoxication in the psychosis cohorts (Table 1): ECA, NEMESIS, NPMS and the Swedish conscripts excluded people with psychosis at baseline; EDSP, Dunedin and CHDS adjusted for baseline symptoms, which the authors note mixes incidence with persistence or relapse; a Swedish analysis restricted to admissions at least 5 years after conscription gave similar results; structural equation modelling in CHDS suggested cannabis predicted later symptoms rather than the reverse. The SCL-90 (CHDS) and the psychosis screening questionnaire (NPMS) cannot identify symptoms caused by intoxication.

Confounding: the psychosis studies adjusted for about 60 different confounders; fully adjusted estimates were smaller than crude ones by an average of about 45% (range 10% to 80%), computed as (crude OR minus adjusted OR) divided by (crude OR minus 1): CHDS 65%, Dunedin 10%, ECA 30%, EDSP 15%, NEMESIS 50%, NPMS 80%, Swedish conscripts 60%. Fixed-effects regression in CHDS for unmeasured stable confounders changed little; adjustment for other substance use attenuated ECA and NEMESIS substantially; in the Swedish conscripts the strongest confounders were IQ, urban upbringing and other mental disorders. Loss to follow-up 4% to 32%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (last column and footnote); Results, 16th and 17th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Consistent with the text by the editors' calculation: the mean of the seven Table 1 values is 44.3%.

key_findings.finding: Depression: 15 cohorts; Egger test p=0.13 (ten studies). Of ten studies with a diagnosis or an above-threshold score, five reported an association persisting after adjustment (two only in subgroups) and no ever-use pool was made because exposure measures differed. More than 230 events would be needed for 80% power to detect an OR of 1.5, so about half the studies were probably underpowered. Most frequent use versus none, pooled adjusted OR 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94), heterogeneity p=0.192, I2 29.6%: CHDS at least weekly 1.70 (1.03 to 2.79), Colombia 1.31 (0.95 to 1.80), ECA 4.00 (1.23 to 12.99), NoRMHS 1.39 (0.32 to 6.02, unadjusted), NPMS dependence 0.90 (0.22 to 3.63), NY state heavy use 1.62 (1.11 to 2.36), Victoria at least weekly, men 0.47 (0.17 to 1.30) and women 1.90 (1.10 to 3.29).
key_findings.note: Comparison: people who did not use cannabis. Adjustment: each study's own model, except NoRMHS (unadjusted, calculated by the reviewers from published tables); outcomes were diagnoses or above-threshold scale scores.

key_findings.finding: Suicidality and anxiety, not pooled: of seven studies of suicidal ideation or attempts, four reported an association in adjusted analyses and one little evidence, and the LA schools cohort reported fewer attempts but more ideation (Figure 5: Baltimore 1.80, 1.02 to 3.17; CHDS 1.43, 1.22 to 1.67; ECA 4.55, 1.37 to 15.11; Chicago men 1.21 and women 0.64, unadjusted). Of seven anxiety studies, two reported an association persisting after adjustment (Figure 6: NY state 1.16, 1.00 to 1.35; Colombia 1.48, 1.10 to 2.00); the ECA obsessive-compulsive disorder association (2.90, 1.11 to 7.57) appeared in a matched sample but not in the whole sample with an unconditional analysis.

Affective studies' handling of bias (Table 2): only four excluded people with affective symptoms at baseline, ten reports adjusted for the baseline outcome, and seven did neither; none explicitly excluded intoxication; five presented only unadjusted results. In six of eight studies with crude and adjusted results, adjustment reduced the association by 10% to 100%; in two (ECA obsessive-compulsive disorder; Baltimore suicidal ideation) it increased. Comprehensive adjustment in CHDS removed associations with depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation, although the depression association persisted at a longer follow-up. Attrition 4% to 70%, median 20%.

The authors judge reverse causation an unlikely explanation for the psychosis associations, because most psychosis studies excluded people with psychosis at baseline, but not for the affective associations; residual confounding can never be eliminated from observational studies; and confounding seems more likely to explain the affective than the psychotic associations.

Population impact and time trends: with about 40% of UK adolescents and young adults having ever used cannabis and a causal OR of 1.4, about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19) of psychotic outcomes in young UK adults would not occur without cannabis; the authors stress that this assumes the association is causal and the pooled estimate accurate. Projected schizophrenia incidence has not followed cannabis trends (Degenhardt et al., ref. 60), but other projections suggest time lags and unreliable incidence data (Hickman et al., ref. 61).
key_findings.note: The method behind the printed interval is not stated. By the editors' calculation, Levin's formula with the pooled interval (1.20 to 1.65) gives about 7% to 21%.

key_findings.finding: Previous syntheses (Table 3): the meta-analyses in Semple et al. (2005), Arseneault et al. (2004) and Henquet et al. (2005) included cross-sectional data, used unadjusted estimates or combined ever use with dependence, and all reported larger effects than this review.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and Discussion, 13th paragraph (p. 326); publication years from the reference list, refs 15, 17 and 19 (p. 327)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: a consistent association between cannabis use and psychotic symptoms, including disabling psychotic disorders, which may result from confounding or bias that cannot be ruled out; enough evidence to inform people that cannabis could increase their risk of a psychotic illness later in life; weaker evidence for affective outcomes. The authors suggest the more pertinent question is whether the evidence justifies policy such as public education. They put individual lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, even with regular use, at less than 3%.
key_findings.note: The less-than-3% lifetime risk has no citation or calculation.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion states that all psychosis studies reporting an association adjusted for other drug use (two not for alcohol), but the Figure 2 footnote marks the EDSP (2.23), NEMESIS (6.81) and NPMS (1.47) most-frequent-use estimates as not adjusted for other drug use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Half the estimates behind the pooled most-frequent-use OR of 2.09 (the summary's dose-response figure) lack adjustment for other drugs; claims should not describe that figure as adjusted for other drug use.

reporting_issues.issue: Four of seven studies of suicidal ideation or attempts are cited as refs 10, 37, 47 and 49; ref. 10 is Renault et al. (1974), a laboratory study of repeated marihuana smoke administration, not a cohort. Figure 5 includes an ECA estimate, so an ECA report (ref. 40 or 41) may have been meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; the cohorts behind the suicidality statement must be identified from Figure 5, not from the reference numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary reports 35 studies, whereas 175 full texts minus 143 exclusions leaves 32 references. The 35 are reports counted per outcome group (11 psychosis + 24 affective): two Dunedin reports (refs 31, 32) are counted in both groups and the affective NPMS data are a personal communication. The reports come from 18 distinct cohorts (7 + 15, with CHDS, Dunedin, ECA and NPMS in both; editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should describe the evidence as 7 cohorts for psychosis and 15 for affective outcomes, not 35 independent studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Figures 3 to 6 are titled as adjusted odds ratios, but footnotes mark some estimates as unadjusted (NoRMHS and NY schools in Figure 3; NoRMHS in Figures 4 and 6; Chicago in Figure 5). The pooled depression OR of 1.49 includes the unadjusted NoRMHS estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled depression estimate is not wholly adjusted; NoRMHS's wide interval (0.32 to 6.02) gives it little weight, so the effect on the pooled value is probably small.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says depression odds ratios for the highest weekly or monthly exposure categories ranged from 1.3 to 1.6, the ECA misuse-disorder study excepted; Figure 4 shows CHDS at least weekly 1.70, Victoria at least weekly 1.90 in women and 0.47 in men, and NPMS dependence 0.90.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text understates the spread of the depression estimates; Figure 4 values should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The population attributable fraction is printed as about 14% (95% CI 7 to 19), and the method for the interval is not stated. By the editors' calculation, Levin's formula with 40% exposure and the pooled interval 1.20 to 1.65 gives about 7% to 21%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the point estimate reproduces, and the figure is conditional on causality in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts of affective studies differ between paragraphs: suicidal ideation or attempts in six studies and anxiety in five plus one (p. 321), but seven studies each later (p. 323). Figure 6 includes NPMS and Victoria (combined depression and anxiety outcomes), which are not among the seven anxiety references cited in the text, while the cited LA schools reports (refs 51, 52) are not in Figure 6.
reporting_issues.consequence: Reports and cohorts are counted interchangeably; study counts for suicidality and anxiety should be taken from the figures with their cohorts named.

reporting_issues.issue: The conflict-of-interest statement lists TJ among those who received honoraria; no author has these initials.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error; the declaration should be reported as printed with this noted.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's column of approximate change from crude to adjusted odds ratio, computed as (crude OR minus adjusted OR) divided by (crude OR minus 1), does not say which exposure contrast each cohort's figure refers to. For NPMS the 80% cannot refer to the ever-use estimate pooled in Figure 1 (adjusted OR 0.72), for which the formula would exceed 100% for any crude OR above 1; it fits the dependence estimate of Figure 2 (1.47) with a crude OR of about 3.35 (editors' calculation). The average of about 45% (range 10% to 80%) given in the text may therefore mix ever-use and most-frequent-use contrasts.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 45% (10% to 80%) describes how much adjustment shrank the cohorts' associations for unstated contrasts; claims should not attach it to the pooled ever-use odds ratio of 1.41 in particular.
